paper_title: Not All Features Are Created Equal: A Mechanistic Study of Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A fine-tuned Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy can easily place the alphabet soup in the basket on command, just as it saw during fine-tuning. However, if the basket is shifted five centimeters to the left, it drops the soup off the table. We developed an interpretability pipeline to investigate what such a policy is computing. Injecting task A's activations into the action expert while the policy looks at task B's scene makes pi0.5 execute task A's motor trajectory in 99.6\% of episodes ($n{=}1{,}968$). The injected program is bound to absolute workspace coordinates and ignores the visible scene, which provides a mechanistic account of the perturbation brittleness that concurrent benchmarks report. The binding holds on a physical UR10e: directed replay redirects the commanded task in 26/26 rollouts in one direction and 18/26 in the other, with no-injection and random-direction controls at the floor, and once the source object is moved 10--15\,cm the arm grasps and releases at the recorded coordinates in 50/50 trials, picking up the wrong block when one sits there and closing on empty air when none does. Applying the same interventions to six VLAs on LIBERO, MetaWorld, SimplerEnv, and ALOHA over 420{,}000+ rollouts yields three further findings: every architecture encodes the instruction, and four of the five weight it below vision whenever the scene alone identifies the goal; under the standard replacement write-back the SAE pooling that preserves behavior is architecture-specific (pi0.5 per-token, SmolVLA indifferent), and goal selection and motor generation separate into VLM and expert pathways wherever the two are distinguishable. We release \textbf{Action Atlas} (https://action-atlas.com), an interactive platform covering all 520+ trained SAEs, 79 identified concepts, and the scored UR10e rollouts. Code: https://github.com/CWRU-AISM/action-atlas

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy [Zitkovich et al., 2023, Kim et al., 2024, Black et al., 2024, Physical Intelligence, 2025, Physical Intelligence et al., 2025] fine-tuned on LIBERO completes more than 90% of trials (Tab. 2). Move the target object few centimeters and success collapses [Zhou et al., 2025, Fei et al., 2025], with the instruction unchanged and the object in plain view. Do VLAs follow the instruction and identify what to manipulate, or do they replay coordinate-bound motor program that hits where the training distribution put the object? When VLA-controlled robot Equal contribution. Corresponding author: pxw206@case.edu 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). misbehaves, operators have no principled way to diagnose the failure beyond behavioral observation, unlike classical robotics whose kinematic and control models are inspectable by construction [Craig, 2018]. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose the dense, polysemantic activations of language models into sparse, monosemantic features [Cunningham et al., 2023, Bricken et al., 2023, Templeton et al., 2024]. At scale they have surfaced safety-relevant representations [Templeton et al., 2024], and support activation steering without retraining [Turner et al., 2023, Rimsky et al., 2024]. Six concurrent studies have opened VLAs with these tools (Tab. 1): Häon et al. [2025] and Buurmeijer et al. [2026] steer scalar kinematics such as speed and height, Swann et al. [2026] and Jin et al. [2026] train SAEs on one policy and suppress or amplify single features, and Miao et al. [2026] raises success along learned subspace. Each edits one direction inside one architecture with the task held fixed, so none can answer the question the perturbation failures pose: when the policy acts, is it executing an instruction about an object or trajectory toward location? single-feature edit cannot separate the two, because object and training-time location co-vary in every learned feature. We separate the two by replacing the computation wholesale  (Fig. 1)  . We record policys residualstream activations while it performs task in scene A, then write them into the forward pass while the same policy looks at scene and is told to perform B. task concept would be reinterpreted against scene and send the arm to Bs object. coordinate-bound program would retrace As path through Bs scene. We run this test across five VLAs (π0.5 [Physical Intelligence, 2025], OpenVLA-OFT [Kim et al., 2025], X-VLA [Zheng et al., 2026], SmolVLA [Shukor et al., 2025], GR00T N1.5 [Bjorck et al., 2025]) and one language-free control (ACT [Zhao et al., 2023]), spanning 80M to 7B parameters, four action-generation paradigms (flow matching, diffusion, continuous regression, and conditional variational autoencoder, CVAE), and four benchmarks (420,000+ rollout episodes). Under this crosstask injection, π0.5 follows the source tasks trajectory in 99.6% of n=1,968 episodes while looking at the destination scene  (Fig. 2)  . Per-model rates, each labeled by metric and reported tie-inclusively, are in Tab. 10. We describe this as coordinate-bound motor program, or an activation-level computation that reproduces the source tasks trajectory shape anchored to workspace coordinates when replayed in new scene. This binding offers mechanistic account of the brittleness pattern reported by Zhou et al. [2025]. Three additional findings repeat across the architectures measured. Language sensitivity depends on task structure. When vision identifies the goal, prompts carry less behavioral weight, even though linear probes read them off the residual stream almost perfectly (4.4). Pathway specialization separates goal selection in the VLM pathways from motor generation in the expert pathways wherever the two are separable. The dissociation is quantified on SmolVLA and reproduced directionally on π0.5 and GR00T, and SmolVLAs interleaved fusion attenuates cross-task override on both LIBERO and MetaWorld (4.5). The SAE pooling preference differs across architectures. π0.5 and OFT require per-token reconstruction, while X-VLA and the GR00T diffusion transformer (DiT) tolerate or prefer mean-pooling and SmolVLA is indifferent. temporal-contrastive arm degrades every architecture by collapsing adjacent latent codes (4.6). Our contributions include: cross-architecture mechanistic analysis of six architectures (80M7B) on four benchmarks under one intervention protocol. Each finding is scoped per model. Causal evidence for coordinate-bound motor programs. Cross-task injection (4.3) and pathway specialization (4.5) jointly localize the substrate, the localization explains the brittleness pattern of Zhou et al. [2025], and the program replicates on physical UR10e (4.7). Empirical guidelines for SAEs on VLA models. three-arm comparison (per-token, mean-pool, temporal-contrastive) across five architectures shows that pooling preference is architecture-tied and that the temporal arm collapses adjacent latent codes (cosadj :0.86 0.997) on every architecture. Action Atlas, an open-source interactive feature-exploration platform (https://action-atlas. com) covering all 520+ SAEs, 79 identified concepts, 10,000+ rollout videos.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: RT-2 [Zitkovich et al., 2023] showed that VLMs can generate tokenized robot actions and set the discrete-token paradigm. OpenVLA-OFT later [Kim et al., 2025] replaced discrete tokenization with continuous L1 regression and achieved 97.1% LIBERO success. parallel line of work dropped autoregressive decoding: π0.5 [Physical Intelligence, 2025] introduced flow matching with dedicated action expert, which avoids the bin-collapse failures of discrete tokens. The six models we study  (Table 6)  span this design space, from 80M (ACT) to 7B (OFT) parameters. Independent robustness evaluations [Fei et al., 2025, Zhou et al., 2025] have shown pattern that our interpretability study explains mechanistically: small object-position perturbations drop OpenVLA and π0 to 0.00 success across all four LIBERO suites and π0.5 to 0.080.38 (vs. 0.920.98 on the unperturbed originals) [Zhou et al., 2025], while instruction-level perturbations drop all three to 0.00 on most suites despite passing semantic paraphrases. Together these failures are consistent with memorizationbased behavior in which the instruction is encoded but not consulted. SAE methods built for language models do not transfer to VLAs unchanged. Per-token preservation matters because action tokens carry phase structure absent in text (4.6), and discrete-token action heads break SAE insertion (App. C.1). Concurrent VLA-interpretability work is single-architecture and single-intervention. Häon et al. [2025] steer π0/OpenVLA feedforward directions for kinematic behaviors such as speed and height on real UR5. Swann et al. [2026] train SAEs on π0.5 and OpenVLA and steer individual features, including object selection under an empty prompt, on DROID hardware. Buurmeijer et al. [2026] steer kinematics and object choice in π0.5 with linear observer-controller on DROID hardware. Miao et al. [2026] gate the action expert toward learned success subspaces, raising task success without changing which task is attempted. Jin et al. [2026] train event-grounded SAEs and report that feedforward-side semantic steering fails to control object choice. Khan et al. [2025] and Molinari et al. [2025] apply SAEs and world-model probes to single policies. Each study edits one direction in one architecture and holds the task fixed. Cross-task injection, the SAE pooling comparison, the pathway separation, and hardware replication are the axes this study adds (Tab. 1). Extended related work in App. A.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We developed closed-loop interpretability pipeline that makes rollout behavior the ground truth for every mechanistic claim  (Fig. 1)  . Activation injection and counterfactual prompting intervene on the policy and read causality from the change in behavior: cross-task activation injection replays recorded computation inside the forward pass, and counterfactual prompting changes the language input while the scene is held fixed. Then, to read out what the network encodes, SAEs decompose the recorded activations into features that localize the causal signal to specific layers and subspaces, and linear probes quantify what the residual stream carries at each layer [Li et al., 2026a]. Validation closes the loop. feature surfaced by the SAEs counts as mechanistic only after it reproduces its effect through the same injection-and-rollout machinery. sections.title: 3.1 VLA Architectures Under Study
sections.content: We study five VLAs and one language-free control: π0.5 [Physical Intelligence, 2025] (3B, flowmatching), OpenVLA-OFT [Kim et al., 2025] (7B, continuous L1), X-VLA [Zheng et al., 2026] (1B, soft-prompted flow), SmolVLA [Shukor et al., 2025] (450M, interleaved VLM-expert), GR00T N1.5 [Bjorck et al., 2025] (3B, DiT-Eagle-VL-SA), and ACT [Zhao et al., 2023] (80M, CVAE, vision-only). Together they span 80M to 7B parameters and four action-generation paradigms: flow matching [Lipman et al., 2023], continuous regression, diffusion, and CVAE decoding (Tab. 6).

sections.title: 3.2 Activation Injection
sections.content: Activation injection extends activation patching [Meng et al., 2022] to full rollout episodes: we replace activations from one episode with those from another during inference. Given source episode (correct prompt, successful rollout) and target episode (alternative condition), we record layer activations {HA,(ℓ)} during A, then at every timestep of override the residual stream at the chosen layers, (1) and let the rest of the forward pass proceed normally. The injection set Linject ranges from single layer to all layers. When prompts and produce residual streams of different sequence lengths, we overwrite only the 50 action-token positions, which are fixed across prompt configurations. When the target runs longer than the recorded source (TB > TA), injection ceases at t=TA and the target policy continues unmodified (<5% of cross-task episodes; restricting to TB TA shifts override 1pp on π0.5 libero_goal). We test three conditions. In null injection, the source episode uses the correct prompt while the target uses an empty string. In same-scene injection, both episodes share the same visual scene but target different objects. In cross-task injection, source and target occupy different visual scenes. For multi-pathway models (π0.5, SmolVLA, GR00T), we also inject into individual pathways to isolate their contributions.

sections.title: 3.3 Counterfactual Prompting
sections.content: We vary text prompts to measure language sensitivity. Each episode is evaluated under one of six conditions: the baseline correct prompt, null prompt (empty string), negation prompt (Dont pick up X), motor command (Move slowly), an object swap (replacing the target object name), and temporal switch (changing the prompt mid-episode). For SmolVLA on MetaWorld, we also test counterfactual prompts across four difficulty levels (easy, medium, hard, very hard).

sections.title: 3.4 Sparse Autoencoders for VLAs
sections.content: We train SAEs on action-relevant activations with TopK sparsity [Gao et al., 2024] (k = 64 active features) and expansion factor = 4d or = 8d. Whether per-token preservation matters depends on architecture (4.6). On π0.5, mean-pooling across the 50 action tokens collapses approach, manipulation, and terminal phases into one vector and drops rollout success from 89.9% to 3.3% (grand mean over the four LIBERO suites; the per-layer libero_object sweep shows the same collapse, 93.8%8.9%) despite normalized MSE 0.05 (R2 > 0.95). We follow Gao et al. [2024] and report normalized MSE. Per-token processing is the conservative default, with per-architecture pooling effects in 4.6 and Appendix H.2. Concept-specific features are identified via frequencyweighted contrastive selection: scoref = df freqf , where df is Cohens [Cohen, 1988] measuring activation difference between concept-present and concept-absent tasks, and freqf is the fraction of samples where feature appears in the active top-k. Across the five VLAs we train 520+ distinct SAEs (per-model counts in Tab. 7), which together identify 79 unique manipulation concepts (union of unique concept names across models; per-model counts overlap heavily) across motion, object, and spatial categories.

sections.title: 3.5 Linear Probes for Action Prediction
sections.content: Linear probes [Alain and Bengio, 2017] test whether action information is linearly decodable from intermediate representations. We train ridge regression probes per action dimension and verify causality by projecting out the probe direction.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: The experiments trace one causal chain: visual context selects coordinate-bound motor program (4.2, 4.3). Language then matters only when vision is ambiguous (4.4), pathway specialization implements that interface, the VLM side choosing the program and the expert side binding it to coordinates (4.5), SAEs read out that substrate under pooling choice that depends on architecture (4.6), and the binding claim is tested on physical arm (4.7).

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We collect 420,000+ rollout episodes across 12 experiment types and up to 50 tasks per environment, on 8A100-80GB, RTX 5090, and 2RTX 4090, over four benchmarks: LIBERO [Liu et al., 2023] (4 suites, 40 tasks), MetaWorld [Yu et al., 2020] (50 tasks, 4 difficulty levels), SimplerEnv [Li et al., 2024b] (10 tasks, 2 embodiments), and ALOHA [Zhao et al., 2023] (2 bimanual tasks). Table 7 summarizes scale.

sections.title: 4.2 Visual Context Dominates Action Generation
sections.content: Visual context dominates action generation across all six architectures (Tab. 2). Injecting baseline visual-pathway activations under null prompt restores cosine similarity to 0.99 and task success to 1480%. Zeroing any single layer sends X-VLA and GR00T-DiT to 0%, while SmolVLA tolerates single expert-layer zeroing (19.276.5% across suites). Recovery is largest for dual-pathway designs (π0.5 7080% per suite at n=50/suite, against matched null controls of 22%, 6.0% and 62%, Tab. 2) and smallest for single-pathway OFT (1415%, n=120 per layer). We attribute the gap to visual-language entanglement, which carries more of the prompt-conditioning load in single-stack architectures (4.4). The recovery is graded and scales with how much the prompt mattered. It restores 88% of the lost success on libero_goal and 69% on libero_object, while the libero_spatial contrast is not significant (p=0.13), the suite where an empty prompt costs only 26 points to begin with. Per-model layer-zeroing profiles in App. H. Within shared scene, same-scene injection of prompt-B activations into prompt-A rollout steers behavior toward the injected target on every multi-pathway model tested, and π0.5 joins SmolVLA in tolerating late-layer zeroing. Vision selects the action, and 4.3 asks what the selected activation encodes.

sections.title: 4.3 Motor Programs Bind to Absolute Spatial Coordinates
sections.content: Does the injected activation encode task concept (pick up the cup) or coordinate-bound motor program? Cross-task injection separates the two. The production condition replaces the expertpathway residual stream at layers 16 and 17 at the 50 action-token positions on every step. Across all five language-capable VLAs, injection collapses destination-task success, and trajectory analysis shows the injected activations steer behavior toward source-task positions (Tab. 3; ACT is the language-free control). Displacement analysis (Figure 2) shows that injection lowers task success and still steers behavior. π0.5, X-VLA, and OFT show strong source-dominant trajectories ( 96% override). GR00T is moderate (57.0% by action cosine, 6.7% by end-effector velocity, Tab. 10), and SmolVLAs expert pathway overrides at 3.07 the VLM-pathway rate (78.6% vs. 25.6%, LIBERO; aggregate 52.1%, n=720). Under injection 6880% of episodes displace an object (>5 mm), but the moved object belongs to the destination scene. DTW on EEF trajectories yields 8691% source-dominance on libero_goal/libero_spatial (App. H.3). norm-matched random direction at the same layers gives 22% source-behavior at n=50 and chance-level override at n=200 (App. C.3), so the override is carried by the injected direction. The robot reaches toward where the source objects would have been, and its motor program is bound to absolute workspace coordinates, consistent with Fei et al. [2025], Zhou et al. [2025]. The binding also holds on hardware (4.7).

sections.title: 4.5 VLM Pathways Select the Goal and Expert Pathways Generate the Motor Program
sections.content: The bind/select division of labor predicts an architectural division, with VLM pathways selecting the goal and motor-expert pathways generating the coordinate-bound motor program. The dissociation is quantified on SmolVLA and reproduced directionally on the other two multi-pathway models. Injecting expert pathways causes active misdirection (reaching to wrong locations), and injecting VLM pathways causes passive stalling (timeout) (Fig. 2, right). On SmolVLA, oracle state-prediction probes recover ground-truth state from expert activations at 4.5 the VLM rate (oracle ratio 0.58 vs. 0.13, Tab. 20). The prediction has two halves, the VLM side decoding the goal better and the expert side decoding the state better. SmolVLA shows the state half and π0.5 the goal half (a modest 14 pp 8 Figure 3: Directed injection on the UR10e. The plushie program is injected at expert L16/L17 under the prompt to stack the blocks. The arm reaches the plushie and carries it to the bowl, and the blocks stay untouched. Tracked points run from start (blue) to end (red). gap): PaliGemma goal classification rises to 76.4% while expert goal classification settles at 62.6% (App. F.1), and GR00T DiT layers are more ablation-sensitive (4080% drop) than VL-SA layers  (Fig. 11)  , consistent with the same expert-encodes-state pattern under different fusion. The goal side is causal. An edit to the VLM pathway at the instruction positions restores goal selection with no instruction on four of five architectures, and matched random or wrong-task edits do not. OFT, which has no separate VLM pathway, does not respond (App. G). Where VLA has separate expert, then, the expert holds the coordinates and the VLM holds the goal, and an edit on the VLM side selects it.

sections.title: 4.6 Pooling Preference Is Architecture-Tied and Temporal Contrast Collapses Phase
sections.content: Reading this substrate with SAEs requires choice of how to pool across action tokens, and the right choice depends on architecture. We train TopK SAEs at each pathway layer (Eqs. 35; 520+ SAEs) and find two cross-architecture patterns. Single-feature ablation has zero effect on 2892% of (concept, task) pairs  (Fig. 7)  , consistent with concepts spread redundantly across many features. Sensitivity concentrates in specific layers, and the action pathway behaves differently from the language stack  (Fig. 5)  : the π0.5 expert (18 layers) and GR00T DiT (16 layers) kill the policy (SR 0.5) on 40% of ablation pairs across most of their depth, while OFT (32 L), X-VLA (24 L), and SmolVLA expert (32 L) keep the kill-switch rate below 10% almost everywhere. Width does not predict sensitivity (per-model profiles in Appendix H). five-architecture three-arm rollout comparison shows two pooling regimes (Tab. 13, rollout success through the per-token and mean-pool SAE). Mean-pooling collapses π0.5 from 81% to 3% and OFT from 80% to 7%, so both require per-token reconstruction. X-VLA (51% to 80%) and GR00TDiT (80% to 83%) do better under mean-pooling, and SmolVLA is indifferent (67.2% and 66.4%). The temporal-contrastive arm collapses adjacent codes (cosadj : 0.86 0.997) at R20.97 on π0.5, X-VLA, and GR00T-DiT (SmolVLA 0.940, OFT data-limited). The collapse and the degradation co-occur on every architecture we ran. The guideline is to choose pooling per architecture and per signal (App. G), and to avoid the temporal-contrastive objective. Mean-pool numbers use the replacement write-back. residual write-back removes the collapse on OFT, GR00T, and X-VLA (App. M).

sections.title: 4.7 The Program Replicates on a Physical UR10e
sections.content: To test the binding claim of 4.3 off the simulator, we fine-tuned π0.5 on Universal Robots UR10e over seven tabletop tasks (76.2% baseline, 160/210) and ran the same wholesale expert replay at L16/L17 between plushie-in-bowl and gray-on-blue stacking, in both directions (App. O). Directed injection (Tab. 5) redirects the commanded task in 26/26 rollouts in one direction and 18/26 in the other, against matched-scene no-injection floors of 0/24 and 0/25 and norm-matched random direction at 0/25 and 1/23. displaced-object test then separates object tracking from coordinate anchoring: with the source object moved 1015 cm off its recorded position, the injected program drives the arm to the recorded coordinates in 50/50 trials across both directions, while the uninjected policy reaches the displaced object. sections.title: 4.8 Limitations
sections.content: Simulation carries all cross-architecture results, and hardware covers one model and one task pair (4.7). Extended limitations and three falsifiable predictions are in App. B.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Across six architectures, fine-tuned VLAs encode coordinate-bound motor programs that the visual pathway selects and, where separate expert exists, the expert pathway executes. Injected at the action expert, source tasks activations carry its trajectory into different scene in 99.6% of π0.5 episodes, and language sensitivity is architectureand task-dependent (4.4). The binding accounts for benchmark brittleness [Zhou et al., 2025, Fei et al., 2025] and replicates on physical UR10e (4.7). The goal lives on the VLM side, where one edit restores it with no instruction on four of five architectures. For SAEs on VLAs, pooling is an architecture-level choice, and the temporal-contrastive objective degrades every architecture we ran.

sections.title: A Extended Related Work
sections.content: A.1 Vision-Language-Action Models RT-2 [Zitkovich et al., 2023] showed that web-pretrained VLMs can be fine-tuned for manipulation via tokenized actions. OpenVLA [Kim et al., 2024] extended this with an open-source 7B model, and OpenVLA-OFT [Kim et al., 2025] replaced discrete tokenization with continuous L1 regression, achieving 97.1% LIBERO success. The π0, π0.5, π 0.6, and π0.7 models [Black et al., 2024, Physical Intelligence, 2025, Physical Intelligence et al., 2025, Physical Intelligence, 2026] introduced flow matching with dedicated action expert and progressively more diverse training context. Whether π0.7s reported emergent capabilities reflect compositional generalization or further-scaled memorized motor patterns is an open question that the mechanistic tools developed here can answer. Current VLAs span several scales and paradigms: SmolVLA [Shukor et al., 2025] (450M), X-VLA [Zheng et al., 2026] (cross-embodiment), GR00T N1.5 [Bjorck et al., 2025] (humanoid), CogACT [Li et al., 2024a], GR-3 [Cheang et al., 2025], VITA-VLA [Dong et al., 2025], SimpleVLA-RL [Li et al., 2026b], RIPT-VLA [Tan et al., 2025], FLOWER [Reuss et al., 2025], SpatialVLA [Qu et al., 2025], and ACT [Zhao et al., 2023] (80M, no language). Modular approaches include SayCan [Ahn et al., 2022], PaLM-E [Driess et al., 2023], and Code as Policies [Liang et al., 2023]. Concurrent representationanalysis work in robot policies uses different tools: Lei et al. [2026] apply UMAP and Wassersteindistance analysis to characterize sim-real co-training, identifying structured representation alignment and importance reweighting effects. Our SAE-based feature-level analysis is complementary. Action Representation. Diffusion Policy [Chi et al., 2023] treats action generation as conditional denoising, 3D Diffusion Policy [Ze et al., 2024] incorporates 3D representations, and FAST [Pertsch et al., 2025] uses DCT-based compression tokenization. Action tokenization directly determines SAE applicability (Section C.1). Language Following. CAST [Glossop et al., 2025] augments robot datasets with counterfactual language labels. VLM4VLA [Zhang et al., 2026] found that VLM benchmark performance does not predict VLA task success, so language understanding and visuomotor competence are decoupled. A.2 Mechanistic Interpretability SAEs [Olshausen and Field, 1997, Bricken et al., 2023, Cunningham et al., 2023, Gao et al., 2024, Templeton et al., 2024] decompose dense activations into sparse interpretable features, with extensions to vision [Stevens et al., 2025, Joseph et al., 2025, Zaigrajew et al., 2025] and vision-language models [Pach et al., 2025]. Activation steering [Turner et al., 2023, Rimsky et al., 2024] enables behavioral control, with advances including conceptor-based steering [Postmus and Abreu, 2024], SAE-guided additions [Soo et al., 2025], and VLM safety steering [Wu et al., 2025, Sivakumar et al., 2025]. Linear probing [Alain and Bengio, 2017, Belinkov, 2022] identifies linearly decodable information, and establishing causal relevance requires intervention [Mueller, 2024]. PvP [Golovanevsky et al., 2025] shows vision and priors compete in multimodal models. 18 A.

sections.title: Interpretability for Robot Learning
sections.content: RT-1 [Brohan et al., 2022] included attention visualizations, Diffusion Policy [Chi et al., 2023] analyzed action distributions, and ALOHA [Zhao et al., 2023, ALOHA 2 Team et al., 2024] demonstrated bimanual manipulation, all without internal representation analysis. RoboFail [Sagar et al., 2024], AHA [Duan et al., 2024], and RACER [Dai et al., 2025] characterize failures behaviorally. Häon et al. [2025] introduced VLA steering via internal representations, Molinari et al. [2025] probed for emergent world models, and Khan et al. [2025] used SAEs to isolate interpretable steering directions in Magma. Interpretability-by-design approaches include CoA-VLA [Li et al., 2025], CoT-VLA [Zhao et al., 2025], TriVLA [Liu et al., 2025b], dVLA [Wen et al., 2025], and Embodied-R1 [Yuan et al., 2025]. Cross-Model and Multimodal SAE Alignment. Per-model SAE training, including ours, leaves features in incompatible per-architecture spaces, which complicates direct comparison of concepts across pathways or models. Two recent lines of work address this. The first scales SAEs across model dimensions: Universal Sparse Autoencoders [Thasarathan et al., 2025] and SPARC [Nasiri-Sarvi et al., 2025] learn single shared dictionary across multiple networks, enforcing concept alignment via shared encoders or global TopK constraint, while Group-SAE [Ghilardi et al., 2024] reduces training cost by tying nearby layers into single dictionary using residual-stream similarity. The second targets multimodal alignment: Kaushik et al. [2026] address the split dictionary phenomenon (where features fire only for one modality) using cross-modal random masking and group-sparse regularization. Both lines are relevant to our setting. The split-dictionary problem mirrors our VLM/expert-pathway split (4.5), and multimodal-aligned SAE can test whether the goal/motor dissociation is orthogonal at the dictionary level or an artifact of independent training. We leave this extension to future work. Concurrent VLA Architectures. Several recent VLA designs explore alternative action-decoding paradigms whose binding behavior our framework can probe directly. On the autoregressive side, AR-VLA [Hu et al., 2026] treats action generation as true causal sequence with long-lived action-history memory, breaking from chunk-based reactive heads. On the flow-matching side, DFM-VLA [Chen et al., 2026] replaces fixed-token decoding with discrete flow-matching iterative refinement, and AsyncVLA [Jiang et al., 2025] introduces asynchronous flow matching with confidence rater for selective regeneration. Bridging the two paradigms, HybridVLA [Liu et al., 2025a] unifies discrete autoregression and continuous diffusion within single LLM backbone. Each design changes the pathway through which an action is produced from visual scene, but the cross-task injection and pathway-zeroing protocols in this paper transfer mechanically. The only architecture-specific concern is the hook placement choice documented in App. D.4. Whether the coordinate-bound binding documented here persists under iterative-refinement (DFM-VLA), confidence-aware regeneration (AsyncVLA), or context-aware autoregression (AR-VLA) is an empirical question that each of these architectures open releases makes testable. We expect the binding to weaken in proportion to how much an architecture re-grounds on the current observation between action chunks, with no commitment to precomputed plan. Single-Policy Diagnostics. VLA-Trace [Shi et al., 2026] traces π0.5 and OpenVLA across checkpoints with kernel alignment and attention knockout and reports strong visual grounding alongside weak fine-grained instruction following, the behavioral pattern of 4.4. LAVLA [Wulff et al., 2026] clusters GR00T N1.5 action-decoder latents layer by layer and finds spatiotemporal and kinematic structure separating in the middle layers. Both analyze one or two policies and do not intervene on task identity. Huang et al. [2026] report the same position-induced collapse of fine-tuned π0.5 on hardware and attribute it to visual-encoder drift. Our probes find grounding intact (>99% decodable), which places the failure downstream in the action pathway.

sections.title: B Limitations
sections.content: Predictions. Treating the substrate as coordinate-bound motor program selected by visual context yields falsifiable predictions. (i) Moving an object out of its training-distribution position should break execution with the instruction unchanged, as robustness benchmarks report [Zhou et al., 2025, Fei et al., 2025]. (ii) Semantic control should require intervening on the pathway that selects the goal. 19 Our pathway-injection asymmetry (expert injection misdirects, VLM injection stalls) is consistent with this, and failed feedforward-side semantic steering [Jin et al., 2026] is the predicted negative result. (iii) Override should weaken as fine-tuning data grows more diverse. Swann et al. [2026] report the feature-level trend. Demonstration count alone does not move override. App. finds it unchanged across 10 range.

sections.title: Benchmark Scope
sections.content: All cross-architecture results come from four simulated benchmarks. The UR10e covers π0.5 on one task pair (App. O) and tests injection and coordinate binding under real sensing and actuation, while visual dominance and pathway specialization remain simulation results. Fine-tuning on new robot reshapes internal representations, so the next step is the same protocol on the other architectures on hardware, with results posted to Action Atlas. Coordinate-Frame Disambiguation Cross-task injection and the displacement analysis (App. H.3) fit binding to absolute workspace coordinates but do not exclude scene-relative coordinates that coincide with the source-task locations. rigid transform of the whole world, exact in simulation, would separate the two, and we have not run it. Under either frame the policy commits to trajectory tied to spatial coordinates and does not re-ground on the visible task, which is what the brittleness account needs, and the physical displaced-object test (4.7) separates object tracking from coordinate anchoring.

sections.title: Counterfactual Prompt Coverage
sections.content: Our counterfactual prompt set tests simple variations (negation, null, swap). Compositional instructions (pick up the red cup, then place it behind the blue bowl) and ambiguous multi-object scenes would provide stronger evidence for language insensitivity claims. Benchmarks like LIBEROPRO [Zhou et al., 2025], which tests corrupted instructions and environmental perturbations, offer stricter evaluation protocol for language grounding. Cross-Task Injection Confounds Injected activations are off-manifold, and temporal misalignment can produce invalid internal states. App. C.3 sets out the three observations that weigh against drift reading: norm-matched random direction at the same layers is at least as far off-manifold and gives chance-level override, displacement places trajectories closer to the source task than to the destination, and on hardware the random arm is the one that moves incoherently (App. O).

sections.title: Concept Identification
sections.content: SAE features are not guaranteed to be disentangled. Ablation validation finds that some identified features encode general motor primitives and lack clean semantic reading.

sections.title: C Methodology Controls
sections.content: C.1 Discrete Tokenization Prevents SAE Intervention Before adopting OpenVLA-OFT, we conducted experiments on base OpenVLA (autoregressive discrete 256-bin tokenization). Despite successful SAE training (R2 = 0.870.96), hooking SAEs into the forward pass produced 0% task success on all but the final layer. The discrete tokenization maps activations to bins via argmax. Even small reconstruction errors shift the selected bin, with errors compounding across the 7-token autoregressive sequence. Replacing discrete tokenization with continuous L1 regression via OpenVLA-OFT enables SAE intervention at 99.2% success. Scale is fixed at 7B, so the action representation sets SAE applicability. C.2 ACT as Non-VLM Control ACT provides control lacking any language pathway. Cross-task injection between TransferCube and Insertion is no-op at this hook (cosine similarity = 1.0, bit-identical action arrays), so ACT 20 gives no cross-task evidence. Grid ablation shows spatially structured representations. Masking grid position (2,2), the primary manipulation workspace, drops success on both tasks (Tab. 2), and Gaussian noise (σ = 0.1) reduces TransferCube to 0% and Insertion to 25%. Visual pathway dominance therefore holds for vision-only policy. Injected source activations are off-distribution by construction. Fitting Gaussian to expert-layer activations from natural rollouts of six libero_goal tasks (8,000 samples per layer) and scoring held-out natural samples against activations injected from the other four tasks, the Mahalanobis distance at L16 is 46.9 injected against 18.0 natural (medians 40.7 and 17.5), with 0.4% of injected samples inside the natural 95th percentile. sections.title: ACT Architecture
sections.content: ACT uses ResNet-18 vision encoder (pretrained on ImageNet) feeding into Transformer EncoderDecoder with CVAE latent space (β = 10, latent dimension 32). The encoder processes multi-view camera observations, and the decoder generates action chunks of 100 timesteps in 14-DOF joint space (7 per arm for bimanual manipulation). D.6 Benchmarks LIBERO [Liu et al., 2023] comprises four suites of 10 tasks each: Goal (different goals in shared scene), Object (pick-and-place with varied objects), Spatial (spatial reasoning and relational placement), and LIBERO-10 (diverse tasks spanning all three categories). MetaWorld [Yu et al., 2020] provides 50 tabletop manipulation tasks grouped by difficulty (easy, medium, hard, very hard). SimplerEnv [Li et al., 2024b] evaluates sim-to-real transfer on Google Robot and WidowX embodiments. ALOHA [Zhao et al., 2023] tests bimanual manipulation with the ACT policy. D.7 Compute Requirements Experiments were conducted on an 8A100-SXM4-80GB cluster for π0.5, OpenVLA-OFT, largescale SAE training, concept ablation, and cross-model analysis, an NVIDIA RTX 5090 (32GB) for GR00T N1.5 experiments, and two NVIDIA RTX 4090s (24GB) for SmolVLA and X-VLA experiments. Total experiment data exceeds 7.1 TB, including 4.3 TB of activation recordings, 152 GB of SAE checkpoints, and 420,000+ rollout episodes. The full study used approximately 10,000 A100 GPU-hours. D.8 Evaluation Protocol Episode counts per condition are stated with each experiment (20 to 50 per task for the main results, 5 per task for the earliest sweeps, and 3 per task for the OFT goal-steering screen). Episodes run for maximum of 300 steps. Cross-Architecture Synthesis Figure 4 condenses the cross-architecture results of 4.24.6 into one view. Each axis maps value from the cited table linearly onto 0100: baseline success, the suite mean of the baseline rows in Tab. 2; visual override, destination success lost under cross-task injection, 100 Dst. SR in Tab. 3; language tolerance, the mean over LIBERO rows of null-prompt over correct-prompt success in Tab. 4, so 100 = prompt-insensitive; SAE fidelity, best-arm rollout success as fraction of baseline in Tab. 13; cross-task transfer, the tie-inclusive override rate (Tab. 10; SmolVLA from Tab. 3, tie fraction 0%); and ablation tolerance, the zero-effect rate of single-feature ablation (Tab. 11, last row). Per-architecture detail is in App. and the SAE pooling results are in App. H. 24 Figure 4: Cross-model summary. Capability radar across the five language-capable VLAs. Each axis maps table value linearly onto 0100, with axes defined in App. E. The pathway-specialization claim of 4.5 rests on three architecture-specific metrics, since no single metric applies to all three multi-pathway models. Component-Level Analysis This section traces information flow below the layer level: individual activation dimensions, FFN neurons, and layer-to-layer representational similarity. We analyze π0.5 in depth (FFN weight projection and LDA on the 1024-dim expert space), then validate across OFT (32-layer neuron-level concept mapping, 80 concepts 11,008 neurons per layer), SmolVLA (FFN neuron contrastive identification on both expert and VLM pathways), and GR00T (per-layer-type SAE feature utilization across DiT, Eagle, and VL-SA). F.1 Goal Encoding Dimensions Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) on π0.5 expert activations at layer 17 identifies three components that separate four goal-suite tasks with 71.9% cross-validated accuracy (n=114, 5-fold). The first component captures 45.8% of discriminant variance, the second 35.2%, and the third 19.0%. The top 20 discriminant dimensions (417, 909, 934, 649, 147, 219, 708, 297, 155, 545, . . . ) define low-dimensional subspace sufficient for goal identification within 1024-dimensional activation space. Goal information emerges at different rates across pathways. PaliGemma goal classification accuracy rises from 56.4% at layer 0 to 76.4% at layer 13, then declines to 68.9% at layer 17. Expert accuracy is flatter: 64.0% at layer 0, peaking at 66.4% (layer 9), settling at 62.6% by layer 17. PaliGemmas steeper emergence profile is consistent with its role as the goal encoder. The expert pathway maintains moderate goal awareness throughout but does not refine it. Individual activation dimensions participate in both goal encoding and action generation. Dimension 62 most strongly modulates the x-component of action output (score 0.074), dimension 618 modulates (0.071), and dimension 14 modulates (0.066). The overlap between goal-discriminant dimensions (417, 909, 934) and action-modulating dimensions (62, 618, 14) is minimal, consistent with separable subspaces for goal identity and motor execution (tested below). Subspace separability via subspace injection. We test separability by injecting only the goaldiscriminant subspace (20 of 1024 dimensions from LDA) from task into task Bs forward pass at layer 17. Across five task pairs on libero_goal, full injection (all 1024 dimensions) causes complete task failure (0% success on 4/5 pairs, down from 100% baseline). Goal-subspace injection (20 dimensions, 2% of the activation space) preserves task success: 100% on three pairs, 67% on 25 fourth where the source and destination share the OPEN motor primitive. Action-subspace injection (15 dimensions encoding x/y/z action components) shows the same pattern. Replacing 2% of the activation space from different task does not disrupt the destination tasks motor execution, evidence for separability of goal identity from motor execution within the same layer, and stops short of direct causal control over goal selection. Additive steering along goal directions in the VLM pathway is tested in App. G. F.2 FFN Motor Primitive Neurons Projecting PaliGemma FFN weight vectors onto token-association vocabulary identifies neurons that encode specific motor primitives. At layer 17, 6,606 of 16,384 neurons (40.3%) associate with motion verbs (pick, place, move, push, pull), 2,907 (17.7%) with object tokens, 2,989 (18.2%) with gripper state, 2,223 (13.6%) with direction, and 1,151 (7.0%) with spatial relations. The distribution shifts across layers. Motion verb neurons increase from 4,231 at layer 0 (25.8%) to 6,606 at layer 17 (40.3%), 56% increase. Gripper neurons triple from 998 (6.1%) to 2,989 (18.2%). Object neurons decrease from 3,660 (22.3%) to 2,907 (17.7%), while spatial neurons decline from 1,655 (10.1%) to 1,151 (7.0%). This progression from object/spatial representation in early layers to motor/gripper representation in late layers traces the computational transformation from scene understanding to action generation within single pathway. OFTs 32-layer Llama-2 backbone shows different pattern. Granular concept mapping (80 concepts per layer, 11,008 neurons) shows that spatial relation neurons (spatial_in: 5,4837,245; spatial_on: 4,7246,727) dominate at all depths and grow monotonically from L0 to L31, while object neurons remain sparse (e.g., obj_can: 8141,175). OFTs 4096-dim representation distributes spatial information broadly across layers, consistent with its resilience to concept ablation (92% zero effect). GR00Ts SAE feature analysis shows layer-type gradient in feature utilization, with later DiT layers using more features. DiT L0 retains only 3,654 of 12,288 features (70% dead), rising to 9,317 alive at DiT L15, while Eagle L0 has 6,730 alive of 16,384 and VL-SA L0 has 11,585 alive. F.3 Layer Similarity via CKA Linear Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) between π0.5 expert layers 5 and 11 on LIBERO-Goal, computed on paired samples (the same rollout steps and token positions in both layers), is 0.79. shuffled-row control gives 0.02. The expert therefore carries shared residual representation that later layers refine, consistent with injected activations persisting through the remaining layers. OFTs 32-layer Llama-2 backbone shows the same refinement pattern from the probing side: R2 for episode-length prediction rises from 0.845 (L0) to 0.941 (L24) before settling at 0.915 (L31), while task classification accuracy saturates at 97.7100% by L8. Combined with the FFN analysis above, these findings indicate that layers in both architectures refine common representation across depth. F.4 Where Spatial Binding Forms During Fine-Tuning Comparing backbone activations between base OpenVLA (fine-tuned with discrete action tokens) and OFT (fine-tuned with continuous L1 regression) on the same LIBERO tasks localizes the representational changes induced by fine-tuning. We feed identical images through both models and measure per-layer cosine similarity of mean activations (n=50 images per suite, 4 suites). Across all four suites, divergence grows with depth. Layers L1L15 remain near-identical (cosine similarity >0.999), L16L28 drift from 0.997 to 0.980, and the final layer L31 drops to 0.9170.938. Layer 0 dips slightly (0.9700.989) from differences in input embedding. The long-horizon libero_10 suite diverges most at L31 (0.917), and the three single-concept suites least (0.9350.938). Fine-tuning therefore reshapes the final third of the backbone and leaves early and middle layers intact. The coordinate-bound programs of 4.3 sit in the layers that change most. 26 Four OFT models fine-tuned on different suites (6 pairs 32 layers, n=30 images each) differ much less at L31 (0.9730.992) and not at all in the middle (L16: 0.9980.999). The action head (discrete against continuous) reshapes late layers more than the choice of fine-tuning suite.

sections.title: G Goal Steering in the VLM Pathway
sections.content: This section tests causally the goal selection that 4.5 places in the VLM pathway. It asks whether an edit there, with no instruction present, makes the policy complete chosen task in scene that holds several possible goals. Protocol. The instruction is replaced by filler string of function words with the same token count, so every other prompt token keeps its position. We record the VLM-pathway residual stream under the true instruction and under the filler, three rollouts each, and edit only the instruction positions (for causal backbones, the instruction and the tokens after it). Three edits are compared. patch replaces the edited positions with their mean under the true instruction. per-position gap adds, at each position, the mean difference between true instruction and filler. single direction adds one unit vector, the gap averaged over positions, scaled to fraction ρ of each tokens norm. Controls are random direction of matched norm and the gap computed for different task. The filler and the true instruction with no edit set the floor and the ceiling. Result. One VLM-pathway edit restores goal selection on π0.5, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and GR00T, and random or wrong-task edits of the same size do not (Tab. 8). OpenVLA-OFT does not respond. On π0.5 single direction at PaliGemma layer 2 completes 113/150 episodes against 6/150 for random direction, and nine of ten tasks respond. Edits at layers 2 and 5 succeed where pilot at layers 9 and 13 failed, so the instruction is read early in the VLM stack. The form of the signal depends on the architecture. π0.5 carries the goal as one direction shared across instruction positions. SmolVLA carries it per position, so one averaged direction fails there at every magnitude. X-VLAs bidirectional Florence encoder spreads the instruction into the image tokens, so the edit has to cover the whole Florence block. GR00T responds to the per-position gap on its Eagle backbone at its ceiling. OpenVLA-OFT runs image and instruction through one Llama stack with bidirectional attention, and the per-position gap over the whole sequence at layer 4 or 12 completes 2/24 episodes on the eight tasks without filler floor, against 24/24 for the true instruction. The same protocol tests whether SAE reconstructions keep the steerable signal (Tab. 9). On X-VLA and GR00T, per-token and mean-pooled SAEs exist at the edited layers, and we add the per-position gap after each one: the per-token SAE reconstructs each position, and the mean-pooled SAE reconstructs the span mean, as it was trained to. On X-VLA the per-token reconstruction steers as well as the raw gap (54/90 against 50/90 at layer 0, Fisher p=0.65), and the mean-pooled reconstruction falls to the random floor (2/90, p=7.51019 against per-token). Pooling the raw gap without any SAE already removes most of the effect. GR00T repeats the pattern. 4.6 finds that X-VLA and the GR00T action head tolerate mean-pooling for rollout reconstruction, and the instruction signal in their language pathway still needs the per-token SAE, so pooling preference also depends on which signal the SAE must keep. On π0.5, direction built from the top 32 features of the per-token PaliGemma SAE recovers 64/150 at layer 5 against 74/150 for the dense direction. H.3 Dynamic Time Warping Analysis of Cross-Task Trajectories The cosine-dominance override metric used in 4.3 (Eq. 2) compares per-step action-vector directions, which is local geometric measure. We add global trajectory-shape measure: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) on end-effector position trajectories, normalized by warping-path length. For each cross-task pair (A, B) with prompt and source As expert activations injected at layers 1617, we compute three DTW distances per episode: dsrc = DTW(xBA-inj, xA), ddst = DTW(xBA-inj, xB), and the inherent dA,B = DTW(xA, xB) as control. We report the fraction of episodes with dsrc < ddst as DTW source-dominance, paralleling the cosine-dominance override rate. DTW corroborates the cosine result on libero_goal (90.7% source-dominance, n=270, Wilson 95% CI [86.7, 93.6]) and libero_spatial (86.4%, n=44). The two metrics agree directionally. The injected trajectory is closer to the source than to the destination on shared-vocabulary suites, both per-step (cosine) and globally (DTW). The 812pp gap between cosine and DTW source-dominance on these suites is expected because cosine measures action-vector direction step-wise while DTW measures trajectory shape globally. An injected episode that briefly aligns with the source then diverges can register as cosine-dominant but DTW-mixed. 31 The long-horizon libero_10 suite shows weaker DTW agreement (45.8% source-dominance vs. 95.8% cosine-dominance, n=24). The inherent dA,B=0.361 is large and injection-induced trajectory truncation often shortens the rollout, making the truncated trajectory artifactually closer to the shorter destination baseline by raw shape distance. Cosine, normalized per-step, is insensitive to this truncation. Because cosine and DTW measure complementary properties, we report both. Agreement on goal/spatial strengthens the source-dominance claim. The libero_10 divergence is documented metric sensitivity to trajectory length under early termination and leaves the cosine result intact. Phase-aligned injection. Most of the override survives any reordering of the source steps, and the order-dependent part is the same under phase alignment and under shuffling. sections.title: Causal Necessity of Linear Probe Directions
sections.content: Linear probes trained to predict action dimensions achieve 9798% R2. Projecting out probe directions eliminates linear decodability by construction (R2 drops to 0). The causal test is 32 behavioral. Rollouts under projection fail (3.5), indicating the network itself relies on information in these directions. Cross-architecture single-feature ablation sensitivity is reported in Fig. 7 (n=15,096 concept-task pairs across five models).

sections.title: Vision Robustness
sections.content: Systematic image perturbation across 6,000+ episodes reveals task-dependent visual robustness. We apply horizontal and vertical flips, rotations (90, 180, 270), center crops (50%, 75%), and object-centric crops. Horizontal and vertical flips break all models tested (0% success), so spatial orientation is rigidly encoded. Rotation and crop robustness varies by task complexity. Simple pick-and-place tolerates mild perturbations while multi-step tasks fail. Object-centric cropping (centering on the manipulation target) outperforms static crops (60% vs. 020%), pointing to reliance on manipulation-relevant regions, with full scene context contributing less.

Setup. We fully fine-tuned π0.5 (20k steps) on Universal Robots UR10e over seven tabletop tasks from 335 teleoperated episodes (60,416 frames at 15 Hz) in the DROID observation format, with two exterior cameras and wrist camera at 320180. Fig. 3 uses the exterior camera facing the robot. Baseline success is 76.2% (160/210, 30 trials per task, three observers), from 66.7% to 86.7% per task. Injection runs only on pairs whose tasks each clear 80% alone, and the headline pair, plushie-in-bowl and gray-on-blue stacking, reaches 86.7% on each. Intervention. The procedure is the simulation procedure unchanged. Captured expert activations at L16 and L17 replace the live ones at each inference call (α=1) under the fixed destination prompt. Flow matching requires matched sampling noise. Wholesale replacement of the expert residual fixes the velocity field, so the denoiser no longer cancels its own initial noise and returns xfinal = asource + (ϵdest ϵsource). On the arm this offset showed up as weak override and an over-scaled gripper, so the physical injector reuses the sources per-call initial noise. In simulation, replaying the sources L16/L17 activations with the sources xT reproduces the source action exactly, and fresh xT leaves an error of 2.18 and 3.73 over two draws (action norm 1.03). The simulation runs behind Tabs. 3 and 26 leave this term uncontrolled. Their override rate compares action directions over full episodes and still reaches 54/54, while the arm executes the raw values. Activation-transfer studies on flow-matching or diffusion heads need to control this term, which discrete and autoregressive heads do not have. Bidirectional override. Each direction ran directed injection, matched-scene no-injection floor, and norm-matched random direction at the same layers and magnitude, with rollouts scored as source, destination, or neither (Tab. 5). Directed intervals exclude both control intervals in both directions, so the effect comes from the content of the injected activations. The 18/26 direction is limited by grasp failure on the compliant plushie. The arm reached for the injected target first in every trial, and the non-source trials diverted only after failed grasp. Displaced-object test. Coordinate anchoring predicts that the arm goes to the recorded position of moved object, vision tracking predicts that it follows the object, and distribution-shift artifact predicts incoherent motion. In 50 trials, 25 per direction, with the source object moved 1015 cm, the arm drove to the recorded coordinates every time and closed on empty air at the vacated position. With two blocks swapped into each others positions it stacks fluently in the wrong color. About centimeter of displacement already makes the grasp fail. Without injection and with the source prompt, the policy reaches the displaced object, so the coordinate locking belongs to the injected program. After the injected sequence ends, the policy cycles fragments of its trained tasks at their trained coordinates. Outcomes are scored behaviorally, with RGB recorded for every rollout.

sections.title: P Broader Impact
sections.content: This work is interpretability research aimed at making VLA decision-making auditable. The artifacts we release (520+ SAE checkpoints, 79 identified concepts, the cross-task-injection rollout corpus, and the feature-exploration platform) are debugging tools and none is deployment-ready policy. All cross-architecture experiments run in simulation, with one physical replication on single task pair (App. O). Positive impact. Mechanistic decomposition supports principled failure analysis. Kill-switch mapping localizes the features and layers VLA depends on, and spatial-binding analysis flags coordinate-grounded brittleness before deployment. The interventional protocols here (null-injection, cross-task injection, single-feature ablation) narrow failure to pathway, layer, or feature subspace. 41 Risks and dual use. Activation injection and feature steering redirect deployed policys behavior without retraining, so an attacker with white-box access to VLAs residual stream can reroute manipulation arm to different target. We mitigate this exposure by releasing interpretability artifacts (SAE checkpoints, rollout videos, and the platform) and no deployable policy or robot control stack. Independently, the coordinate-bound binding documented in 4.3 is itself deployment hazard. VLAs that pass simulation benchmarks fail under modest scene-position perturbations [Zhou et al., 2025]. Practitioners deploying VLAs for high-stakes tasks should run perturbation-style robustness benchmarks [Zhou et al., 2025, Fei et al., 2025] before deployment. Compute and energy. Total compute and data volume are reported in App. D.7. All training used existing pretrained VLA checkpoints, and we do not pretrain new VLAs.

Answer: [Yes] Justification: The four claims listed in the abstract and Section 1 (visual pathway dominance, suite-dependent language sensitivity, coordinate-bound motor programs via cross-task injection, and per-token vs. mean-pool vs. temporal-contrastive SAE pooling) are each supported by named experiments in Sections 4.24.7 with sample sizes, p-values, and Wilson 95% CIs reported. 2. Answer: [Yes] Justification: dedicated Limitations appendix (Appendix B) discusses benchmark scope (simulation for the cross-architecture results, one physical UR10e replication in Appendix O), counterfactual prompt coverage, cross-task injection confounds, the coordinate-frame control not run, and concept identification caveats, with steering sensitivity reported in Appendix H.
